items.subject: math
items.question: Suppose $X_1 = \{u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n\}$ and $X_2 = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ are subspaces of a vector space $V$. Why does it follow that $u_i + u_j \in X_1$ for all $1 \le i, j \le n$?
items.answer: Because a subspace is closed under scalar multiplication, so multiplying u_i by any scalar stays inside X_1.
items.referenceAnswer: Because $X_1$ is a subspace of $V$, it is closed under vector addition; thus, the sum of any two vectors in $X_1$ (including basis or spanning elements $u_i, u_j$) must also lie in $X_1$.
missedPoints: The student incorrectly cites scalar multiplication instead of vector addition.
The question asks specifically about why u_i + u_j ∈ X_1, which relies on closure under addition, not scalar multiplication.
The reference answer correctly identifies closure under vector addition as the key property.
items.feedback: You confused closure under scalar multiplication with closure under vector addition. Review the definition of a subspace: it must be closed under both operations, but only addition explains why u_i + u_j stays in X_1. Focus on the two axioms of subspace closure separately.

items.subject: math
items.question: Given $u_i \in X_1$ and $v_i \in X_2$, and scalars $\alpha_i, \beta_i$, why is $\alpha_i u_i + \beta_i v_i$ an element of $X_1 + X_2$?
items.referenceAnswer: Since $\alpha_i u_i \in X_1$ and $\beta_i v_i \in X_2$, their sum belongs to the sum of subspaces $X_1 + X_2 = \{x_1 + x_2 \mid x_1 \in X_1, x_2 \in X_2\}$ by definition.

items.subject: math
items.question: Let $u = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i u_i + \sum_{i=1}^n b_i v_i$ and $v = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i u_i + \sum_{i=1}^n d_i v_i$. Show that $\alpha u + \beta v$ can be written as a linear combination of the $u_i$'s and $v_i$'s with coefficients expressed in terms of $\alpha, \beta, a_i, b_i, c_i, d_i$.
items.referenceAnswer: Expanding: $\alpha u + \beta v = \sum_{i=1}^n (\alpha a_i + \beta c_i) u_i + \sum_{i=1}^n (\alpha b_i + \beta d_i) v_i$, which is a linear combination of the $u_i$'s and $v_i$'s.

items.subject: math
items.question: Why is $[X_1 \cup X_2]$ a subspace of $V$? Briefly justify using closure properties.
items.referenceAnswer: Because any linear combination of vectors from $X_1 \cup X_2$ can be expressed as a sum of combinations from $X_1$ and $X_2$, and the resulting vector lies in $[X_1 \cup X_2]$, satisfying closure under addition and scalar multiplication.

items.subject: math
items.question: If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are subspaces of $V$, what does the notation $X_1 + X_2$ represent, and how is an arbitrary element of $X_1 + X_2$ expressed?
items.referenceAnswer: $X_1 + X_2$ denotes the set of all sums $x_1 + x_2$ where $x_1 \in X_1$ and $x_2 \in X_2$. An arbitrary element is $\alpha_i u_i + \beta_i v_i$ for some scalars $\alpha_i, \beta_i$ and vectors $u_i \in X_1$, $v_i \in X_2$.
